pedagogy.summary: Locating a/b on a number line by partitioning the unit interval 0–1 into b equal parts (each of length 1/b) and iterating a of them from 0. The number line recasts a fraction as a NUMBER with a magnitude and a position, not a shaded region. The critical shift is to count equal INTERVALS (lengths from 0), not tick marks or dots, and to treat the 0–1 segment as the unit.
bestPractices: Partition the 0–1 interval into b equal parts and emphasise the LENGTH from 0 (the magnitude) rather than the tick mark.
Iterate the unit fraction: 3/4 is three 1/4-jumps from 0.
Make explicit that b equal parts need b−1 marks inside the interval (fourths = 3 interior marks), countering the tick-counting error.
Use lines that extend past 1 so a/b sits among the numbers and cannot be pushed 'between 3 and 4' (IES Roadblock 2.2).
Do both moves — read the fraction at a given point (interpret) AND place a given fraction on a blank line (produce).
Contrast with the area model and stress that the same fraction is 'the same size / the same point'.
keyRepresentations: Single 0–1 number line partitioned into b equal intervals
Stacked 0–1 number lines (IES Figure 4, halves through tenths)
Fraction strips measured against the line (IES Figure 5)
commonMisconceptions: Counting tick marks instead of intervals / drawing b marks rather than b−1 interior marks (IES Roadblock 2.1)
Whole-number placement — putting 3/4 between 3 and 4, treating numerator and denominator as separate whole numbers (IES Roadblock 2.2)
Treating the whole drawn segment (0 to the far end) as the unit rather than 0–1
Reading a point by matching to marks with no sense of the unit-fraction length

learn.summary: Help children locate a/b on a number line by partitioning the 0–1 interval into b equal parts (each of length 1/b) and iterating a of them from 0. The number line recasts a fraction as a NUMBER with a magnitude and a position, not a shaded region. The key shift is counting equal INTERVALS (lengths from 0), not tick marks or dots, and treating the 0–1 segment — not the whole drawn line — as the unit. Learners should both read a fraction at a given point and place a given fraction on a blank line.

activities.title: Build fourths: three cuts, not four marks
feedback: If 3/4 is placed too far from 0, count the equal jumps from 0: 'how many jumps of the same size?' — three quarter-jumps, landing before 1.

If fourths are drawn with 4 interior marks, shade each piece and count LENGTHS, not marks: four interior marks make five parts (fifths if equally spaced), but four equal parts need only 3 cuts inside.
If a point is read off by one (e.g. calling it 4/5), re-count the equal intervals from 0 rather than the ticks.
activities.rationale: Partitioning into b equal parts with b−1 interior marks and iterating the unit fraction directly attacks the common tick-counting error; letting the child see that four marks produce fifths, not fourths, makes the correction concrete.
sourceClaims: Number lines should be used to teach fractions as numbers with magnitude; students commonly count tick marks rather than intervals (Roadblock 2.1) and apply whole-number knowledge by placing e.g. 3/4 between 3 and 4 (Roadblock 2.2). Recommendation 2 (number lines) is rated moderate evidence.
learnerActions: Start with a bare line labelled only 0 and 1 — the 0–1 segment is the unit.

To make 'fourths', first try the common mistake: drop FOUR equally spaced marks inside the 0–1 segment. Notice this cuts the unit into FIVE equal parts, each one a fifth (1/5) — the far interior mark sits at 4/5. So you have actually made fifths, not fourths: a sign something has gone wrong.
Correct to THREE interior marks so the unit is cut into exactly four equal parts (quarters); the marks land at 1/4, 2/4, 3/4, and a fourth quarter-length jump lands exactly on 1 (4/4).
State the rule in your own words: b equal parts need b−1 interior marks.
Place 3/4 by jumping the quarter-length three times from 0, landing one quarter-length short of 1.
activities.intendedInsight: Four equal parts require three interior cuts (b equal parts need b−1 interior marks); a/b is measured as a LENGTH from 0 (a jumps of 1/b), not as a count of tick marks. Drawing four equally spaced interior marks cuts the unit into five equal parts (fifths), so calling them fourths mislabels the pieces — making the tick-counting error visible so the child can correct it.

activities.title: Read the point, then place the fraction
feedback: If the point is read as 4/5, re-count the equal intervals from 0 — the marks are not the count; the lengths are.
If 3/4 is placed beyond 1, ask 'where is 1? must 3/4 be less than 1 or more than 1?' and place it inside 0–1.
If a child can read on a marked line but struggles on a blank one, rebuild the partition step by step before placing.
activities.rationale: Doing both moves — interpret a shown point and produce a placement on a blank line — consolidates the magnitude idea and exposes whether the child relies on pre-drawn marks.
sourceClaims: Number lines should be used to teach fractions as numbers with magnitude; students commonly count tick marks rather than intervals (Roadblock 2.1) and apply whole-number knowledge by placing e.g. 3/4 between 3 and 4 (Roadblock 2.2). Recommendation 2 (number lines) is rated moderate evidence.
Pupils are taught to recognise and use fractions as numbers and to place them on a number line during KS2 (Years 3–4, ages 8–9).
learnerActions: On a 0–1 line already divided into 6 equal parts, with a dot on the 4th mark from 0, say what fraction the dot shows and explain how you know (four 1/6-lengths from 0 = 4/6).
On the same line, find and mark 1/2 (the 3rd mark, i.e. 3/6) and explain why it sits halfway.
Then take a blank 0–1 line and place 3/4 yourself: partition into 4 equal parts, count 3 parts from 0, land three-quarters of the way to 1.
Talk through each step aloud as you place it.
Also try ordering several fractions along one line to compare their positions.
activities.intendedInsight: Reading a given point (interpret) and placing a given fraction on a blank line (produce) are both needed; a fraction is the same size / the same point however it is represented.

activities.title: Which segment is the unit?
feedback: If 3/4 lands at three-quarters of the entire drawing, find and mark 1 first, then measure the quarter-length against the 0–1 segment only.
If a child says 3/4 would move when the line reaches 2, point back to the fixed 0–1 unit — the quarter-length is unchanged.
activities.rationale: Explicitly locating 1 and using lines that run past 1 help expose and address both the whole-segment-as-unit error and the whole-number placement of 3/4 beyond 1.
sourceClaims: Number lines should be used to teach fractions as numbers with magnitude; students commonly count tick marks rather than intervals (Roadblock 2.1) and apply whole-number knowledge by placing e.g. 3/4 between 3 and 4 (Roadblock 2.2). Recommendation 2 (number lines) is rated moderate evidence.
learnerActions: On a line that extends past 1 (to 2 or beyond), first find and mark where 1 is.
Place 3/4 and check it sits below 1, NOT at three-quarters of the whole drawn line.
Answer: if this line went all the way to 2 instead of 1, would 3/4 move? Explain why not.
State that everything is measured against the fixed 0–1 length, whatever the drawing shows.
activities.intendedInsight: The unit is the 0–1 segment, not the whole drawn picture; with 0 and 1 kept in place, a/b keeps its position no matter how far the line is drawn. Lines extending past 1 let children show, and teachers address, errors such as placing 3/4 at or beyond 1, or 'between 3 and 4'.

activities.title: Compare with the area model
feedback: If the child treats the area-model and line versions as different fractions, lay a fraction strip whose whole matches the 0–1 length against the line so the shaded length and the marked point coincide.
Prompt: 'Is 3/4 a different amount on the line than in the rectangle? Why or why not?'
activities.rationale: Contrasting the area model with the line while stressing identical magnitude links prior representational knowledge to the number-line view and guards against seeing them as unrelated.
learnerActions: Shade 3/4 of a rectangle using the area model, then place 3/4 on a number line.
Explain how both show the same fraction — 'the same size, the same point'.
Measure a fraction strip against the line, using strips whose whole is the same length as the line's 0–1 segment, so the length and the position match (e.g. the 1/6 strip against sixths on the line).
activities.intendedInsight: The same fraction has one magnitude whether shown as a shaded region or as a point/length on a line; connecting the two representations reinforces that a fraction is a single number.

constraints: A pre-labelled reference line (tap a point → 'this is 3/4, three quarter-jumps from 0') supports recall but does not let the child partition or iterate, where the learning lives; use it as a scaffold only, not as the main task.
Both interpret (read a shown point) and produce (place on a blank line) are required; recognition alone does not elicit the independent partitioning and placement that demonstrate understanding.

A number line is one-dimensional; the unit-interval idea lives on a single line, so added dimensions are not needed for this particular objective (this is a scope note, not a claim that other media cannot teach).
Children aged ~8–9 (KS2 Years 3–4) are the intended audience; keep lines and partitions simple (halves through tenths).

When an interactive builder is used, optional feedback such as rejecting an unequal drag, a 'hopper' that jumps the unit fraction and lands on a/b, a draggable point that reports the nearest fraction and turns green on the exact spot, and a mode showing the line running past 1 can make the mechanism concrete — these are illustrative, not mandatory or proven superior to other media.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
One source (DfE National Curriculum) was marked verified:false in the original; treat its curriculum-placement claim with that caveat.

Arithmetic correction made during review: drawing four interior marks cuts the 0–1 unit into FIVE equal parts (fifths, each 1/5), with the far interior mark at 4/5 — it does NOT overshoot past 1. Three interior marks make four quarters (marks at 1/4,2/4,3/4), and a fourth quarter-length jump lands exactly on 1 (4/4).

The original recommendation's claim that the far mark 'lands on 5/4' when four marks are dropped is a confused/erroneous original detail: 5/4 would require five quarter-length jumps (keeping the interval at 1/4), not four interior marks. It is recorded in uncertainty notes and not presented to learners.

Verified examples after correction: 4/6 reads as four 1/6-lengths from 0; 1/2 = 3/6 sits at the 3rd mark; 3/4 sits three-quarters toward 1, just before 1; three interior marks make four equal quarters; four interior marks make five equal fifths (far mark 4/5).

The original error-pattern note 'reads the 4th mark... calls the point 4/5' is retained only as a plausible tick-counting slip used in feedback as an off-by-one example to re-count, not taught as a fact; it has not been independently verified.

probeDeeper: How many equal parts did you make, and how many marks did you draw inside — why is that one fewer than the number of parts?
Where is 1 on your line? Is 3/4 before or after 1, and how do you know?
This point is 4/6. Can you find and mark 1/2 on the same line?
If this line went all the way to 2 instead of 1, would 3/4 move? Why not?
assess.correctAnswer: The dot is 4/6 — four 1/6-lengths from 0. To place 3/4: partition 0–1 into 4 equal parts (3 marks inside), then count 3 parts from 0, so 3/4 sits three-quarters of the way to 1, just before 1.

errorPatterns.pattern: Counts tick marks not intervals — reads the 4th mark as if the marks were the count, or makes 4 interior marks to show fourths
errorPatterns.nextMove: Shade each interval and count LENGTHS from 0 ('how many jumps of the same size?'); make explicit that b equal parts need b−1 interior marks
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Off-by-one reading of the point, or partitions with the wrong number of marks when producing

errorPatterns.pattern: Whole-number placement — puts 3/4 between 3 and 4, treating the fraction as two separate whole numbers
errorPatterns.nextMove: Firmly label 0 and 1; ask 'where is 1? must 3/4 be less than 1 or more?'; place it inside 0–1
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On the blank line places 3/4 beyond 1, near where 3 or 4 would be

errorPatterns.pattern: Treats the whole drawn segment as the unit — ignores the 0–1 labelling and measures a/b as a fraction of the entire picture
errorPatterns.nextMove: Find and mark 1 first; establish that the unit is 0–1, and everything is measured against that fixed length whatever the drawing shows
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On a line drawn past 1, places 3/4 at three-quarters of the total drawn length rather than of 0–1

responseLevels.gap: Counts tick marks or places 3/4 beyond 1 / at three-quarters of the whole drawing; cannot identify the 0–1 unit interval.
responseLevels.full: Reads the point as 4/6 by counting equal intervals from 0, and independently partitions 0–1 into b equal parts and iterates a of them to place 3/4 correctly below 1, explaining the unit interval and the interval length.
responseLevels.partial: Reads or partitions correctly on a marked line but falters when producing on a blank line, or gets the position without articulating that each interval is 1/b and the unit is 0–1.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Show a 0-to-1 number line already divided into 6 equal parts, with a dot on the 4th mark from 0. Ask: 'What fraction is this dot, and how do you know?' Then give a blank 0-to-1 line and ask: 'Mark 3/4 on this line, and talk me through how you place it.'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who treats the 0–1 segment as the unit and counts equal intervals reads 4/6 and places 3/4 correctly below 1. The tick-counting child miscounts marks (calls the point 4/5, or draws 4 marks for fourths); the whole-number-placement child pushes 3/4 out beyond 1 (toward '3 to 4') or places it at three-quarters of the whole drawing. Both moves — interpret and produce — are needed to pass.
